candidate.hook: If your squat stalls above parallel, don’t blame your hips—the real handbrake is your ankles. Gain a few degrees of dorsiflexion and your depth appears without changing anything else.
candidate.frame: We’ve all hammered hip mobility, but the squat lives or dies at the ankle. View this through an ankle-first lens—tibia angle and dorsiflexion set your balance and torso mechanics, which is why depth shows up when the ankles open.

When dorsiflexion is restricted, the knees hit a hard stop, forcing the hips back and the torso to lean to maintain balance—compensations that cap depth even if the hips are mobile (per Macrum et al. 2012). Remove that constraint and depth often appears: elevating the heel or wearing weightlifting shoes permits greater knee flexion and a more upright, deeper squat without changing the hips (per Sato et al. 2012). If you want to predict or improve depth, screen the ankle first with a weight-bearing lunge test—it’s reliable and responsive to change—and program dorsiflexion-focused work or a small heel wedge as needed (per Konor et al. 2012; Powden et al. 2015). Hip mobility still matters for comfort and pelvic control, but for most “stuck above parallel” lifters, a few extra degrees of ankle dorsiflexion unlock the knee and torso angles that make deep squatting possible (per Macrum et al. 2012; Sato et al. 2012).
